endorsements.title: Adoption of AI in Healthcare Delivery Systems: Early Applications and Impacts
endorsements.quote: There is mixed feedback on the impact of ambient scribe on clinician time saved. Standardized metrics and deeper research would support understanding.

endorsements.title: Ambient technology in epilepsy clinical practice
endorsements.quote: Future prospective studies must be undertaken to concretely establish the advantages of using AmI models.

endorsements.title: Using ambient AI in clinical consultations: reframing policy around clinical audit and patient safety
endorsements.quote: Benefits should therefore be measured locally rather than assumed and, consistent with WHO guidance on AI for health, must not be allowed to accrue mainly to well-resourced, dominant-language settings ( 11 ).

endorsements.title: A Conceptual Model for Ambient AI Adoption: Perspectives From Academia and Industry
endorsements.quote: Quantitative data may include changes in documentation time, note completeness, coding patterns, message turnaround times, or visit length.

endorsements.title: Embracing Large Language Models for Medical Applications, Part II: Building a Framework for Clinical Stewardship.
endorsements.quote: They should also be evaluated for note accuracy, concision, clinician time, patient trust, billing effects, and differential performance across specialties, languages, accents, and visit types.

evidence.title: The Influence of Artificial Intelligence Scribes on Clinician Experience and Efficiency among Pediatric Subspecialists: A Rapid, Randomized Quality Improvement Trial
evidence.outcome: Clinician experience, burnout, pajama time, note time, and wRVUs with ambient scribe versus control
evidence.effect: KLAS Net EHR Experience rose 52.6 to 75.2 in intervention vs 37.3 to 30 in control; burnout fell 89% to 56%; no significant change in pajama time, note time, or wRVUs.
evidence.quote: Among pediatric subspecialists, AI scribes improved clinician experience and burnout without changing charting time or EHR work outside work hours.

evidence.title: Ambient AI Scribes in Clinical Practice: A Randomized Trial
evidence.outcome: Local ambient scribe effect on time-in-note, burnout, task load, accuracy, and usability versus control
evidence.effect: Nabla reduced time-in-note 9.5% (95% CI -17.2% to -1.8%; P=0.02); DAX no significant change (-1.7%). Both scribes suggested improved Mini-Z, task load, and work exhaustion; occasional inaccuracies reported.
evidence.quote: Nabla users experienced a 9.5% (95% CI, -17.2% to -1.8%; P=0.02) decrease in time-in-note versus the control group, whereas DAX users exhibited no significant change versus the control group (-1.7%; 95% CI, -9.4% to +5.9%; P=0.66).

evidence.title: A Pragmatic Randomized Controlled Trial of Ambient Artificial Intelligence to Improve Health Practitioner Well-Being
evidence.outcome: Ambient scribe effects on well-being, note time, documentation quality, and billing codes in local randomized trial
evidence.effect: Work exhaustion/interpersonal disengagement -0.44 points (95% CI -0.62 to -0.25); time on notes -0.36 hours/day; PDSQI-9 mean scores 3.97 to 4.99 of 5; diagnostic billing codes improved (P<0.001).
evidence.quote: Documentation time decreased without compromising diagnosis, billing compliance, or note quality.

evidence.title: Comparing ambient scribes: a randomized crossover clinical trial addressing ambient scribe technologies' impact on physician burnout
evidence.venue: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
evidence.outcome: Local assessment of ambient scribe usability, clinician well-being, and time savings
evidence.effect: Both tools reduced personal and work burnout and improved workflow satisfaction; product B reduced minutes-in-notes more (-3.19 min); no meaningful differences in pajama time or patient-related burnout.
evidence.quote: Both tools reduced personal and work burnout scores, but differences between tools were not meaningful.

evidence.title: Hybrid Ambient Clinical Documentation and Physician Performance: Work Outside of Work, Documentation Delay, and Financial Productivity
evidence.outcome: After-hours work, documentation delay, and wRVU productivity after ambient scribe activation
evidence.effect: WOW rose 32.1% at day 10 then fell 41.7% by day 50; odds of delayed notes fell 66.0% at day 50; wRVUs rose 12.1% by day 50.
evidence.quote: ACD adoption was associated with reduced after-hours work, faster note completion, and improved financial productivity within 50 days of implementation.
evidence.sample_unit: clinicians (attending physicians and advanced practice clinicians)

evidence.title: Ambient Artificial Intelligence Versus Human Scribes in the Emergency Department
evidence.outcome: Local ambient scribe evaluation of note quality (PDQI-9), EHR time, and physician note contribution versus human scribes
evidence.effect: PDQI-9 similar for adults, lower for pediatrics with AI (41.36 vs 42.25, aRR -1.89 [95% CI -3.58 to -0.20]); more EHR notes time with AI (adult 4.3 vs 1.8 min).
evidence.quote: PDQI-9 scores were similar for adults, but AI scribes scored lower for pediatric patients (41.36 versus 42.25, adjusted risk ratio [aRR] = -1.89 [95% confidence interval (CI) -3.58 to -0.20]).

evidence.title: Changes in Clinician Time Expenditure and Visit Quantity With Adoption of Artificial Intelligence–Powered Scribes
evidence.outcome: EHR time, documentation time, and weekly visit volume after AI scribe adoption versus non-adopters
evidence.effect: AI scribe adoption associated with 13.4 (95% CI, 9.1-17.7) fewer minutes of EHR time, 16.0 (13.7-18.3) fewer minutes documentation time, 0.49 (0.17-0.81) additional weekly visits; after-hours EHR time unchanged.
evidence.quote: In a difference-in-differences analysis, AI scribe adoption was associated with 13.4 (95% CI, 9.1-17.7) fewer minutes of EHR time, 16.0 (95% CI, 13.7-18.3) fewer minutes of documentation time, and 0.49 (95% CI, 0.17-0.81) additional weekly visits delivered.

evidence.title: Integrating AI Scribe Technology into Public Health Workflows: Simulation and Field Evaluation in Disease Case Management
evidence.venue: Studies in health technology and informatics
evidence.outcome: Documentation time with AI scribe versus usual practice at two public health units
evidence.effect: At SMDHU, scribe use was associated with a mean reduction of 12.9 minutes in documentation time compared with usual practice (p < 0.05), whereas at WDGPH it was associated with a mean increase of 10.4 minutes (p < 0.05).
evidence.quote: At SMDHU, scribe use was associated with a mean reduction of 12.9 minutes in documentation time compared with usual practice (p < 0.05), whereas at WDGPH it was associated with a mean increase of 10.4 minutes (p < 0.05).

evidence.title: Ambient scribe in general practice: a multi-perspective before-after longitudinal mixed-methods study
evidence.outcome: Clinical documentation time, consultation time, documentation quality, GP and patient experience after ambient scribe
evidence.effect: Documentation time decreased by 42.7 seconds (95% CI -56.29 to -30.78, p<0.0001); total consultation time not different (-61.4 s, p=0.069); GPs reported reduced workload; inaccurate summaries noted.
evidence.quote: Clinical documentation time decreased by 42.7 seconds (95% CI [-56.29; - 30.78], p<0.0001).

evidence.title: Impact of an AI medical scribe after 375 000 notes generated across care levels in a European health system
evidence.outcome: Local ambient scribe assessment of usability, clinician well-being, and time savings
evidence.effect: Documentation time per note decreased 29%; stress-free work rose from 2.41 to 3.14; presence with patients rose from 3.73 to 4.33; median editing time 93 seconds.
evidence.quote: On a five-point Likert scale, the ability to work without stress related to administrative tasks increased from a mean of 2.41 to 3.14 (p = 2.46e-8), and perceived presence with patients increased from 3.73 to 4.33 (p = 2.47e-8).

evidence.title: Artificial Intelligence-Generated Draft Replies to Patient Inbox Messages
evidence.outcome: Time measures, clinician task load and work exhaustion after AI draft reply pilot
evidence.effect: No change in reply action, write, or read time; task load score fell 61.31 to 47.26 (P<.001); work exhaustion fell 1.95 to 1.62 (P<.001).
evidence.quote: There was no change in reply action time, write time, or read time between the prepilot and pilot periods.

evidence.title: The Effect of Ambient Artificial Intelligence Notes on Provider Burnout
evidence.outcome: Clinician burnout and professional fulfillment (Stanford PFI) before and after ambient scribe pilot
evidence.effect: Median burnout score improved from 4.16 to 3.16 (p = 0.005); burnout rate fell from 69 to 43%; interpersonal disengagement 3.6 vs 2.5 (p<0.001); work exhaustion and fulfillment (6.1 vs 6.5, p=0.10) not significant.
evidence.quote: Results showed a significant reduction in burnout scores, with the median burnout score improving from 4.16 to 3.16 (p = 0.005), with validated Stanford PFI cut-off for overall burnout of 3.33.
evidence.sample_unit: clinicians (physicians and advanced practice providers completing pre and post surveys)

evidence.title: Evaluation of an Ambient Artificial Intelligence Documentation Platform for Clinicians
evidence.outcome: Local ambient scribe assessment of usability, clinician well-being, time in notes, and workload before and after implementation
evidence.effect: Time in notes per appointment fell from 6.2 to 5.3 minutes (P<.001); NASA-TLX mental demand 12.2 to 6.3; burnout 42.1% to 35.1% (P=.12); benefit varied by sex and specialty.
evidence.quote: Mean (SD) time in notes per appointment significantly decreased from 6.2 (4.0) to 5.3 (3.5) minutes (P < .001), with a bigger decrease for female vs male clinicians (8.1 [3.9] to 6.7 [3.6] minutes vs 4.7 [3.5] to 4.2 [3.1] minutes; P = .001).

evidence.title: Ambient Artificial Intelligence Scribes in Oncology: Adoption, Feasibility, Acceptability, and Appropriateness
evidence.outcome: Local ambient scribe pilot assessing adoption, feasibility, acceptability, appropriateness among oncology providers
evidence.effect: Providers used the scribe in 620 (13.9%) of 4,449 visits; 17 of 18 survey respondents (94%) used AI-drafted content at least sometimes; 11 (61%) desired continued access.
evidence.quote: Out of 18 survey respondents, 17 (94%) indicated they used the AI-drafted content at least sometimes, demonstrating feasibility.

evidence.title: Evaluating artificial intelligence ambient voice technology as a documentation assistant in psychiatry: proof-of-concept study
evidence.outcome: Local ambient scribe assessment of documentation time, clinician-rated accuracy, quality, efficiency, and well-being
evidence.effect: Median administration time fell from 27 min (manual) to 10 min (AVT) (P<0.001); AVT took 45% of manual time; clinician-rated accuracy, quality and efficiency significantly higher.
evidence.quote: The median administration time per clinical encounter reduced from 27 min (manual) to 10 min (AVT) (P < 0.001).

evidence.title: Quality of Clinical Notes Created by Ambient Listening Generative AI: Pragmatic Prospective Pilot Study
evidence.outcome: Local assessment of ambient scribe documentation accuracy and quality via physician review of notes
evidence.effect: Local pilot review of 356 notes identified error types and severity; 94.7% (337/356) free from significant errors, showing feasibility of local evaluation.
evidence.quote: Prior to deploying an AI scribe, organizations should pilot the technology and include an efficient review process to understand the nature and type of errors common at their organization.
evidence.sample_unit: AI-generated clinic notes evaluated by physicians

evidence.title: Reduction of Electronic Medical Record Documentation Time and Burden Using an Artificial Intelligence Scribe Tool in an Orthopaedic Clinic
evidence.venue: The Journal of the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons
evidence.outcome: Active EMR time per clinic day and per patient before versus after AI scribe implementation
evidence.effect: Total active EMR time per clinic day decreased 26.1% (339.1 vs 458.8 min; P<0.0001); per-patient time decreased 35.3% (7.7 vs 11.9 min; P<0.0001).
evidence.quote: Total active EMR time per clinic day significantly decreased by 26.1% after implementation (after: 339.1 ± 78.7 vs. before: 458.8 ± 95.6 minutes; P < 0.0001).

evidence.title: Implementing Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Ambient Documentation Technology for Ambulatory Clinicians: An Innovation Evaluation
evidence.outcome: Local pre-post documentation time savings with ambient scribes
evidence.effect: 0.35-min-per-note and 2.07-min-per-day reduction in documentation time versus the prior 3-month period.
evidence.quote: Compared to the 3-month period immediately prior to initiating the ambient trial, clinicians experienced a 0.35-min-per-note and a 2.07-min-per-day reduction in documentation time.

evidence.title: Medical Scribe and Ambient Artificial Intelligence Impact on Emergency Physician Documentation Burden and Clinical Productivity
evidence.outcome: Attending documentation time and productivity (wRVUs per shift hour) with ambient AI scribe versus no scribe
evidence.effect: Ambient AI scribes associated with 1.6-minute reduction in adjusted median attending documentation time per note (95% CI 0.3 to 2.9); human scribes 3.3 minutes (2.3 to 4.3); wRVUs per shift hour did not differ.
evidence.quote: Compared with encounters with no scribe, ambient AI scribes were associated with a 1.6-minute reduction in adjusted median attending documentation time per note (95% confidence interval 0.3 to 2.9), whereas human scribes were associated with a 3.3-minute reduction (95% confidence interval 2.3 to 4.3).

evidence.title: Pre-Post Evaluation of Documentation Burden, Time Perception, and Cognitive Workload of Ambient AI Scribe Tools
evidence.venue: AMIA Joint Summits on Translational Science proceedings. AMIA Joint Summits on Translational Science
evidence.outcome: Perceived documentation time, after-hours work, cognitive workload, and objective EHR documentation minutes after ambient scribe pilot
evidence.effect: Perceived documentation time and after-hours work fell significantly (all p < 0.001, r = 0.73-0.80); NASA-TLX domains decreased (g = 0.76-1.54); objective EHR documentation minutes did not change (t(15) = 1.52, p = 0.15, g = 0.36).
evidence.quote: These findings suggest that ambient AI scribes meaningfully reduce perceived workload and improve calibration of documentation burden, even when measurable documentation time remains stable.

evidence.title: Using an Ambient Artificial Intelligence Tool to Document Clinical Pharmacist Patient Encounters: Real-World Evidence From a Federally Qualified Health Center
evidence.venue: Journal of the American College of Clinical Pharmacy : JACCP
evidence.outcome: Documentation time and clinical productivity after ambient scribe implementation among pharmacists
evidence.effect: 31.17% reduction in median time documenting notes per day (38.5 vs. 26.5 min, p = 0.04); visit increases not statistically significant.
evidence.quote: Nine ambient AI documentation tool users demonstrated a 31.17% reduction in median time spent documenting notes per day (38.5 vs. 26.5 min, p = 0.04).

evidence.title: Selecting, Scaling, and Measuring the Value of Ambient AI in a Nonacademic Health System: Multiphase Pilot Study
evidence.outcome: Local pilot assessment of documentation time and patient satisfaction after ambient scribe deployment
evidence.effect: 35.4% decrease in pajama time (P=.054) and 28.3% decrease in time in notes (n=23; P<.001); patient satisfaction improved across domains (all P<.001).
evidence.quote: The pilot showed a 35.4% decrease in pajama time (P=.054, trend toward significance) and a 28.3% decrease in time in notes (n=23; P<.001).

evidence.title: Real-world evaluation of an ambient AI scribe in Spanish outpatient care after 2.3 million uses: impact on clinician experience, semantic agreement, and workflow efficiency
evidence.outcome: Local ambient scribe assessment of accuracy (semantic agreement), usability, clinician experience, time savings
evidence.effect: Semantic agreement 87.4-89.2%; consultation duration 15.01 vs 14.65 min; clinician experience improved in five of seven domains (g = 0.25-0.41)
evidence.quote: Semantic agreement remained high and stable (87.4-89.2%).

evidence.title: Nurse-Led Ambient AI Scribe for Patient Safety Incident Investigation Reports (Project NARRATE): Retrospective Pre-Post Comparative Document-Quality Study
evidence.outcome: adapted PDQI narrative quality
evidence.effect: The cluster-adjusted mean difference for the adapted PDQI mean score was 0.53 points higher for AI-supported reports (95% CI 0.37-0.69; P<.001).
evidence.quote: After accounting for multiple reports contributed by the same supervisor, the cluster-adjusted mean difference was 0.53 (95% CI 0.37‐0.69; P <.001) points.

evidence.title: Large-Scale Implementation of Ambient Artificial Intelligence Documentation and Its Effects on Electronic Health Record Efficiency and Clinician Well-Being
evidence.outcome: Ambient scribe effects on documentation time, usability, clinician well-being, and satisfaction
evidence.effect: Active note time fell from 5.54 to 4.09 min per appointment (26.2% reduction; p<0.001); survey (n=233) reported reduced burnout, increased satisfaction and work-life balance. Documentation accuracy was not assessed.
evidence.quote: Compared with the preimplementation period, active note time decreased significantly (5.54-4.09 min per appointment; 26.2% reduction; p < 0.001).

evidence.title: Human vs. artificial intelligence in medical charting: a comparative study in the simulated emergency medicine context
evidence.outcome: Ambient scribe documentation time, edit burden, and clinician preference versus dictation in simulated ED
evidence.effect: Mean dictation time 2:05 min vs 1:15 min AI note editing (39% savings, p < 0.0001); 69% of 240 sections needed no edits; 63% preferred AI note.
evidence.quote: Mean dictation time was 2:05 min compared to 1:15 min for AI note editing, representing a 39% time savings (p < 0.0001).

evidence.title: Rapid Evaluation of Artificial Intelligence Technology Used for Ambient Dictation in Primary Care: Comparing the Quality of Documentation of Artificial Intelligence-Generated and Human-Produced Clinical Notes
evidence.outcome: Ambient scribe note quality (modified PDQI-9) versus human-produced notes, blinded raters
evidence.effect: Human notes scored higher than AI in all 5 cases; low back pain case human 43.8 vs AI 20.3, difference -23.5 (CI -29.2 to -17.9); AI lower in all 10 domains.
evidence.quote: Notes generated by AI had lower-quality scores than human-generated notes across 5 standardized care cases.
evidence.sample_unit: AI scribe tools (notes rated by 30 blinded raters across 5 standardized cases, compared with 18 human note takers)

evidence.title: Feasibility of Tailoring Artificial Intelligence-Assisted Ambient Scribes for Intensive Care Unit Rounds: Algorithm Development and Validation
evidence.outcome: Local assessment of scribe documentation accuracy, quality (PDQI-9), and error severity
evidence.effect: Accuracy 69% vs 80%; PDQI-9 35.8 vs 38.3 (P=.06); most errors no to low harm potential; time savings and well-being not measured.
evidence.quote: Finally, in terms of overall readability and usefulness, M6 was better than M1 based on PDQI-9 scores, but the difference was not statistically significant (M1=35.8, SEM 0.78 vs M6=38.3, SEM 0.53; P =.06).

evidence.title: Comparative evaluation of ambient digital scribe systems in clinical documentation
evidence.venue: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
evidence.outcome: Whether clinician Likert ratings of scribe quality align with transcript-level error audit
evidence.effect: Clinician ratings did not track audit error counts; physicians flagged hallucinations more often than the audit confirmed ('pseudo-hallucinations'). After Bonferroni correction only Vendor A vs B on short visit remained significant (P=.0098).
evidence.quote: In this sample, clinician preference did not track audit-identified error counts, raising the hypothesis that note-style features influence ratings alongside documentation correctness; larger samples are required.

evidence.title: Ambient Artificial Intelligence Scribes: A Pilot Survey of Perspectives on the Utility and Documentation Burden in Palliative Medicine
evidence.outcome: Documentation time savings with ambient AI scribe versus dictation, by resident
evidence.effect: One resident had a significant reduction in documentation time (p < 0.025); a second resident saw essentially no improvement. Benefit was uneven across the two clinicians.
evidence.quote: One resident saw a statistically significant reduction (p < 0.025) in the time spent on clinical documentation, while a second resident saw essentially no improvement.

evidence.title: Psychiatric Documentation and Management in Primary Care With Artificial Intelligence Scribe Use
evidence.outcome: Documentation of neuropsychiatric symptoms (RDoC) in AI-scribed vs other notes
evidence.effect: Estimated RDoC symptom levels in all 6 domains significantly greater in AI-scribed notes compared with other groups.
evidence.quote: Estimated levels of RDoC symptoms in all 6 domains were significantly greater in the AI-scribed notes compared with other groups.

evidence.title: Ambient AI scribe in pediatric outpatient visits: documentation burden, quality, and scale-up limits
evidence.outcome: Ambient scribe documentation quality, usability, corrections needed, time, and uneven adoption across clinicians
evidence.effect: Documentation quality improved (overall median 23 vs 17; p=0.008), but 67% reported technical issues, 33% needed extensive corrections, and adoption was under one-third of trained clinicians.
evidence.quote: Fifty-five percent of users reported being satisfied or very satisfied, although 67% reported technical issues and 33% reported requiring extensive corrections.

evidence.title: Navigating Collective Bargaining Barriers to the Implementation of AI Scribe Technology Among Ambulatory Advanced Practice Providers: Mixed Methods Quality Improvement Study
evidence.outcome: Variability in scribe use and note content retention across clinicians
evidence.effect: Individual use ranged 30% to 89% (SD 16.9%); retained AI note content averaged 78% (SD 18.2%; range 20%-93%)
evidence.quote: Individual use ranged from 30% (54/179) to 89% (501/563; SD 16.9%).

evidence.title: Enhancing Clinical Documentation Workflow with Ambient Artificial Intelligence: Clinician Perspectives on Work Burden, Burnout, and Job Satisfaction
evidence.outcome: Whether ambient scribe benefit differed across clinician specialty or duration of use
evidence.effect: Specialty type and number of days using the tool did not significantly affect survey responses; ease of documentation OR 6.91 (95% CI 3.90 to 12.56).
evidence.quote: Clinician specialty type and number of days using the AI tool did not significantly affect survey responses.

evidence.title: Physician Perspectives on Ambient AI Scribes
evidence.outcome: Physician perceptions of scribe accuracy, style, workload, and time
evidence.effect: Positive on cognitive demand (16 of 16 comments, 100%), temporal demand (62%), overall workload (89%); accuracy and style largely negative, particularly note length and editing requirements.
evidence.quote: Physician perspectives on accuracy and style were largely negative, particularly regarding note length and editing requirements.

evidence.title: Subjective and objective impacts of ambulatory AI scribes
evidence.venue: The American journal of managed care
evidence.outcome: Perceived versus actual documentation time change after AI scribe adoption
evidence.effect: 86.5% perceived DocTime reductions, but no overall association between perceived and actual change (OR 0.975; P=.144); actual savings uneven, concentrated in physicians with higher baseline DocTime.
evidence.quote: Although the majority of physicians perceived reductions in DocTime (86.5%) following AI scribe adoption, there was no overall association between perceived reductions and actual changes in DocTime (OR, 0.975; P  = .144).

evidence.title: AI-Powered Ambient Scribe Technology Experiences Among Emergency Physicians: Cross-Sectional, Mixed Methods Pilot Survey Study
evidence.outcome: Emergency physician trust in ambient scribe note accuracy, efficiency, usefulness by note component
evidence.effect: Trust in accuracy 6/14 (42.9%) vs 6/8 (75%) for in-person scribes; efficiency improved 10/14 (71.4%); helpful for physical exam 3/13 (23.1%), MDM documentation 5/14 (35.7%).
evidence.quote: However, only 42.9% (6/14; 95% CI 22.3%-69.2%) of respondents trusted the accuracy of ambient scribe-generated notes, compared with 75% (6/8; 95% CI 40.9%-92.9%) who trusted in-person scribes.

evidence.title: Improving Clinical Efficiency Using Artificial Intelligence Scribe for Documentation (ICE-AID Study): A Retrospective-Prospective Cohort Study at a Quaternary Children's Hospital and Health Service
evidence.venue: Journal of paediatrics and child health
evidence.outcome: Clinician-rated document quality of AI scribe notes (modified PDQI-9 domains)
evidence.effect: Median score 4 on a 1-5 scale in 9 of 10 survey domains (n = 77), indicating acceptable quality; mean SUS 74.
evidence.quote: The document quality survey showed acceptable document quality with median score 4, in 9 of the 10 survey domains (scale 1-to-5, n = 77).

evidence.title: Implementation of an AI-Assisted Workflow for Rehabilitation Discharge Summary Creation: Evaluation of Documentation Efficiency, Usability, and Hallucinations in a 290-Bed General Hospital in Japan
evidence.outcome: Local assessment of AI documentation accuracy, usability, and time savings after deployment
evidence.effect: Documentation time fell from median 23.0 to 10.0 minutes (-12.26 min, p<0.001); median SUS 83.75; but 81.8% of summaries contained at least one error.
evidence.quote: The adjusted linear mixed-effects model revealed a significant reduction of 12.26 minutes (95% CI: -15.71 to -8.81; p<0.001).
evidence.sample_unit: post-implementation rehabilitation discharge summaries (documentation time); 18 therapists for SUS; 11 summaries for hallucination review

evidence.title: Deployment of an ambient AI scribe in emergency care: A 12-month evaluation in a large Spanish hospital network
evidence.outcome: Documentation quality and benefit consistency across physicians using an ambient scribe
evidence.effect: Audits showed higher documentation quality scores for Scribe reports, with a large effect size and consistent improvements across physicians; consultations 21.8% shorter.
evidence.quote: Audits of clinical reports showed higher documentation quality scores for Scribe-generated reports, with a large effect size and consistent improvements across physicians.

evidence.title: Large language model-based scribing tools for ophthalmology: performance and safety evaluation using simulated clinical encounters
evidence.outcome: Ambient scribe documentation accuracy and quality across six tools
evidence.effect: Heidi AI highest PDQI-9 (38.524), then Whisper GPT-4o (38.048); all tools produced errors, especially omissions of critical details.
evidence.quote: However, persistent errors, particularly omissions of critical details, were observed across all tools and could compromise patient care.

evidence.title: Feasibility of Tailoring Artificial Intelligence-Assisted Ambient Scribes for Intensive Care Unit Rounds: Algorithm Development and Validation
evidence.outcome: ambient scribe documentation errors
evidence.effect: Errors occurred despite M1/M6 accuracies of 69.12%/80.32%; omissions averaged 15.5%, partial errors 7.2%, and commissions 2.6%.
evidence.quote: Overall, errors of omission were most common (mean 15.5%, SEM 2.7%), followed by partial errors (mean 7.2%, SEM 0.92%) and then errors of commission (mean 2.6%, SEM 0.7%).

commentary.bottom_line: Local evaluations of ambient scribes, including four randomized trials, show that such assessment can be done and that time savings, accuracy, and adoption differ across sites, products, and clinicians. No study tested whether local assessment itself changes deployment decisions or reduces documentation errors reaching patients.

perspectives.view: Four randomized trials and many pre-post studies evaluated ambient scribes within local deployments, which shows that local assessment can be done. No study compared organizations that evaluated locally with those that did not. Time-in-note results were inconsistent across trials, and well-being measures improved more consistently. Indirectness limits certainty for the practice to low.

Few studies measured accuracy, and one pre-post study of 210 providers did not assess it. Physician review of 356 local notes found 94.7% free of significant errors, while a Japanese deployment found 81.8% of 11 summaries had at least one error. Simulated ICU rounds showed omissions averaging 15.5%. Error rates appear to vary by setting.

At two Canadian public health units, scribe use was associated with a 12.9-minute reduction at one and a 10.4-minute increase at the other. In one trial Nabla cut time-in-note 9.5% while DAX did not change it. Among 310 physicians, perceived and actual time savings were not associated, which suggests evaluations may need objective EHR measures alongside surveys.

One study of 100 clinicians found benefit varied by sex and specialty, and a two-resident study found gains for one resident only. A safety-net study included nine pharmacists, and Swedish and Spanish studies evaluated non-English documentation. No test reported outcomes for Medicaid, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients.

Uptake varied, which affects the return on any evaluation effort. Oncology providers used the scribe in 13.9% of 4,449 visits, fewer than one-third of trained clinicians adopted it in a Spanish study, and individual use ranged from 30% to 89%. In one emergency department, AI scribes were associated with more EHR note time than human scribes (4.3 vs 1.8 minutes for adults).

One pilot reported improved patient satisfaction across domains after deployment, but most studies measured clinician outcomes only. One endorsing source asks that benefits not accrue mainly to well-resourced, dominant-language settings. Patient experience and patient-detected errors are largely absent from the evaluation measures tested so far.

commentary.research_gap: No study tests whether conducting a local assessment leads to different adoption decisions, earlier detection of documentation errors, or fewer errors reaching patients, compared with deploying without one. Standardized accuracy audits, patient-reported outcomes, and subgroup analyses by clinician type and patient population are rarely included in the local evaluations published to date.
commentary.underserved_note: One test included a safety-net setting (nine pharmacists), and studies from Sweden, Spain, and Japan evaluated non-English documentation. No test reported results for Medicaid patients, patients with limited English proficiency in English-dominant settings, or low-literacy patients, so current local evaluation methods may not detect accuracy problems or uneven benefit in these groups.
